newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Buba's Welteke says sees no EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Welteke says sees no EMU delay.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke on Wednesday dismissed speculation about a delay to Europe's planned single currency and said he believed the project could get under way with only a small start group.
"I continue to believe that European Economic and Monetary Union will start on January 1, 1999," Welteke told reporters during a conference organised by the Austrian National Bank.
Asked if he thought EMU could get off the ground with only a few participating states, Welteke replied: "Yes...The main thing is that (the single currency) gets started."
His remarks appeared to widen a split with his Bundesbank colleague Reimut Jochemsen who said on Tuesday the prospect of a weakling European currency would be worse than a delay.
The European Union is due to make its final decision on which countries make the grade for monetary union in 1998, basing their selection on 1997 economic data.
Welteke did not advocate softening EMU entry rules but he cautioned against placing undue emphasis on a budget deficit ceiling of 3.0 percent of gross domestic product.
"There is nothing about 3.0 percent in the Maastricht Treaty," he said, adding that he believed a sustainable budget deficit was a more significant goal.

He echoed comments made on Tuesday by his Austrian colleague, National Bank director Adolf Wala, who said the sustainability of budget deficits was more important than strict adherence to the three percent deficit criteria.
European Union member states had already made progress in achieving price and exchange rate stability, as foreseen in the Maastricht Treaty, Welteke said.
"It was clear from the beginning that some small countries have a problem with the debt criteria. We have to look at the whole picture," he added.

Asked whether he believed Britain, under a new Labour government, would be among the first countries to introduce a single currency, Welteke said: "Britain does not want to. We cannot force Britain to take part."
Labour has pledged to hold a "real national debate" on the pros and cons of joining a single currency and to hold a referendum before taking any decision.
